page: Amazon Web Services m5.4xlarge is a general-purpose instance powered by the AWS Nitro hypervisor. It features an Intel Xeon 8175M processor utilizing the x86_64 architecture, providing 16 dedicated vCPUs across 8 physical cores with hyper-threading enabled. The CPU operates at a clock speed of 3.1 GHz and includes 33 MB of L3 cache. The instance is equipped with 64.0 GB of DDR4 memory running at 3 GHz, yielding a balanced 4.0 GB of RAM per vCPU. It does not include local storage or dedicated GPU hardware, and it offers a baseline network bandwidth of 5 Gbps.

Benchmark data indicates a clear performance profile. Single-core performance is relatively weak, as shown by bottom-quartile results in stress-ng single-core, Geekbench single-core, and single-threaded gzip compression tests. However, multi-core performance scales to average levels, with stress-ng multi-core, Geekbench multi-core, and Passmark CPU tests all scoring in the middle 50%. Memory bandwidth for both cached and uncached reads and writes also performs in the average tier. For specialized tasks, the instance handles Redis SET operations, static web serving, and small-model LLM text generation at average speeds, though prompt processing on medium-sized models falls into the lower performance tier.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the m5.4xlarge offers a balanced distribution of compute and memory resources using mature DDR4 and Intel Xeon hardware. This resource density makes it a practical choice for workloads that do not require high-speed local NVMe storage or cutting-edge single-core speeds. It is well-suited for general-purpose applications, multi-threaded software compilation, static web serving, database operations, and moderate Redis caching layers.
description: Amazon Web Services m5.4xlarge is a general-purpose instance featuring 16 dedicated vCPUs and 64.0 GB of DDR4 memory, running on an Intel Xeon 8175M processor at 3.1 GHz under the Nitro hypervisor. It lacks local storage and GPU accelerators, relying on network-attached storage and offering a baseline network bandwidth of 5 Gbps. Performance benchmarks reveal a tradeoff: single-core execution speeds are weak, falling in the bottom 25%, whereas multi-core performance and memory bandwidth consistently reach average tiers. This makes the instance highly capable for multi-threaded tasks but less optimal for single-threaded bottlenecks. Qualitatively, the hardware profile offers balanced resource density for standard enterprise applications. It is best suited for workloads such as static web serving, database operations, multi-threaded software compilation, and general-purpose business applications.
